variants.name: Abstract pure-virtual view interface (classic)
variants.idiom_name: abstract class IView with pure virtual members + presenter holding IView&
variants.implementation_notes: The textbook realization: declare an abstract IView with pure virtual display/query methods, implement it in the concrete window class, and give the presenter a reference to IView and to the model. All C++-specific care goes into lifetime and dispatch: keep the view outliving the presenter (or re-attach explicitly), give IView a virtual destructor, and wire gesture callbacks to presenter methods only after construction so the derived view is fully built. This is the default because it needs nothing beyond the standard library and keeps the view contract explicit and reviewable.
pitfalls: The view must outlive the presenter or be re-attached explicitly; a dangling IView& is undefined behaviour and nothing (no GC) keeps it honest.
Calling virtual view methods from a constructor of a base/derived pair dispatches to the base version only - wire presenter callbacks after construction.
Deleting a view through a base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behaviour; the widget hierarchy makes this easy to hit.

variants.name: Qt QObject signals and slots
variants.idiom_name: QWidget view with signals/slots + QObject presenter connected with QObject::connect
variants.implementation_notes: Qt replaces the hand-written interface callbacks: the view is a QWidget subclass whose user gestures emit signals (or connect built-in widget signals), the presenter is a QObject with slots, and QObject::connect ties them together with compile-time-checked function-pointer syntax. Qt automatically disconnects when either side is destroyed, which removes the manual detachment the classic form needs, and the presenter still holds no widget types if signals carry plain values. Choose this when Qt is the project's toolkit and its event loop is already running; keep the pure-virtual form when the screen must also be testable without linking Qt.
pitfalls: A single-threaded event loop: blocking or long-running work in a slot freezes the UI; move it to a worker thread and return via a queued connection.
QObject must be used from its thread; a presenter touched from another thread needs moveToThread or queued signal delivery.
Lambdas connected without a context object are not disconnected when the view dies; pass the receiver as the context argument to QObject::connect.

variants.name: std::function callback members
variants.idiom_name: view struct holding std::function members assigned by the presenter
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of a virtual interface, the view can be a plain struct whose members are std::function callbacks that the presenter assigns (showTotal = [this](double t){ ... }), and whose query side is provided as ordinary callables. This removes the vtable and the inheritance requirement, lets lambdas close over whatever they need, and makes the wiring site show exactly which behaviour is connected - useful for small screens, headers-only components and non-inheriting widget types. Prefer the pure-virtual interface when the contract is large or several view implementations must be substituted by type, since std::function hides signature mismatches until call time.
pitfalls: An unassigned std::function throws std::bad_function_call when invoked - initialise every member or check it before calling.
Capturing by reference ([&]) in a callback that outlives the enclosing scope dangles; capture by value or keep the referents alive for the view's lifetime.
std::function adds an allocation for large captures and erases the concrete type, so error messages and debugging are less precise than a virtual interface's.
